ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: ALLS participants are young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, mainly aged 18, but up to age 21, at W1.
They were recruited by local research assistants who found eligible individuals at schools, church groups, and community events.

To take part in the study, participants provided written informed consent, then they completed the first survey either on an electronic tablet carried by a research assistant, on paper, or via a link sent to participant's device.

Participants were recontacted for subsequent waves either online or in-person via local research assistants, which allowed for a more representative sample compared to an online-only study in these contexts.
At W1, 3,048 young adults were recruited to participate in ALLS.
Participants were, on average, 18.32 years old (SD = 0.76), with 58% reporting having completed high school and 36% reported to be looking for employment.

> At W1, 3,048 young adults were recruited to participate in ALLS.

> Participants were, on average, 18.32 years old (SD = 0.76), with 58% reporting having completed high school and 36% reported to be looking for employment.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: At W1, 3,048 young adults were recruited to participate in ALLS. At W2, approximately 700 participants dropped out of the study or could not be reached again so a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3. For the present analyses, we restricted the sample to participants who took part in W7 and in either W1 or W3. Furthermore, we excluded participants who failed to pass attention check items (e.g., "Which of the following is a building?", with response options house, tree, plane, cat, and book). Applying these exclusion criteria led to a final sample of N = 2,770. With this sample size, we had a sufficient power of 80% to detect very small personality-outcome associations of r = .053 (Champely, 2006; Funder & Ozer, 2019).

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Personality-Outcome Links in Sub-Saharan Africa
table.research_questions:
Although there are reasons to believe that findings from Western countries might not generalize to the three sub-Saharan countries (Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa), the existing research nonetheless serves as a useful starting point for the formulation of hypotheses. Table 1 provides an overview of findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries. Furthermore, we also included one longitudinal study on personality-outcome associations that was conducted in sub-Saharan Africa in this table (Kura et al., 2025).

Based on this existing evidence and the conceptual overlap of different personality taxonomies, we then developed hypotheses for the present study (see Table 2). Specifically, Extraversion, Openness, and low negative emotions (Emotional Stability) are components of Agency, while Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and even-temper (Emotional Stability) are components of Communion (Thalmayer, Mather, et al., 2024). 

(Table 1 and 2 have been uploaded as separate files to the Design plan section of this preregistration to ensure readability)
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will use data from Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer, Asatsa, et al., 2024), an ongoing longitudinal study conducted in sub-Saharan Africa with surveys every 6 months. For this study, we will use data from W1 to W7, which have been collected between January 2022 and April 2025.

ALLS was addressed to young adults (aged 18 to 21) from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Eligible individuals were identified with the help from local research assistants who recruited potential participants via local networks, community events, and high schools. After providing written informed consent, participants completed the surveys of the different assessment waves on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants’ devices, or on paper. Each wave comprised questionnaires about participants’ personality traits, well-being, mental health, and demographic variables. All questionnaires were provided in English. More details about the study design of the ALLS can be found in Thalmayer, Asata, et al. (2024).

For the present study, we will use data on the Big Two personality traits collected at W1 and W3 and data on life outcomes collected at W7. 68188ba7aceb5a48ea5ef82d Tables_Preregistration.pdf https://osf.io/project/5zw4a/files/osfstorage/68188ba7aceb5a48ea5ef82d https://osf.io/download/68188ba7aceb5a48ea5ef82d 1c0a25894fbb700b2a379b3a73cb051d8531b82fcb5857f7e41c782ec8090667
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: Data from the ALLS have been used in three previous publications (Haehner et al., 2025; Kura et al., 2025; Thalmayer, Mather, et al., 2024). These publications examined the structure, correlates, and changes of personality traits in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Furthermore, one study also examined longitudinal correlations between Big Six personality traits and anxiety, depression, and mental health at W5 (Kura et al., 2025). Thus, there are initial insights on personality-outcome associations for some traits and outcomes. However, the study by Kura and colleagues (2025) used a different personality inventory, different assessment waves and a different statistical approach compared to the ones used here. Specifically, data from W7 has only recently been collected and has not been analyzed before.
table.data_collection_procedures:
ALLS included participants (a) living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, (b) aged between 18 and 21 years at W1, and (c) speaking basic English. 
Participants were recruited from rural villages, towns and urban areas, including from informal settlements. Local research assistants reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools. 
The study used a combination of online and paper-pencil methods for data collection. Many participants had to be re-contacted in person via the local research assistants for each assessment wave. This procedure allowed to collect a more representative sample compared to online-only studies as internet access varies across the three countries.
To compensate for dropout, booster samples were added to the study at W3 following the same data collection procedures.
table.sample_size:
Overall, 3’048 individuals took part in W1 of the ALLS. However, 700 individuals could not be reached again at W2 and a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3.
For the present study, we will restrict the sample to individuals who took part in either W1 or W3 and W7. Furthermore, we will exclude data from measurement occasions where participants failed to pass attention check items. The final sample size for our analyses thus still has to be determined.
table.sample_size_rationale: We expect a final sample size of approximately N = 1800 individuals. With this sample size and a level of significance of 5%, we will have a power of 93% to detect a small effect of a personality-outcome association (i.e., corresponding to an effect size of R2 = 1%).
table.stopping_rule: Not applicable as data has already been collected.
table.measured_variables:
Big Two personality traits (assessed at W1 and W3): assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory (Thalmayer, Mather, et al., 2024): The 45 Items (e.g., “I tend to be calm”) were assessed on a 6-point response scale ranging from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate)

Life outcomes (assessed at W7):

- Subjective well-being assessed with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985): Three items (e.g., “I am satisfied with my life”) were assessed on a 7-point response scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree)

- Self-reported health: “In general, would you say your health is...” rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent)

- Depression and anxiety assessed with the depression and anxiety subscales of the International Mental Health Assessment (Thalmayer et al., 2023): Items (e.g., “I felt scared” were assessed on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (not in the last month/never) to 7 (daily)

- Relationship status: “Are you in a romantic relationship?” assessed with five response options: 0 = I am not in a relationship, 1 = I am in a relationship but do not live with my partner, 2 = I am in a relationship and live with my partner, 3 = I am married, 4 = Other
-> Recoded as 0 = no relationship (former option 0), 1 = in relationship (former options 1 to 3)

- Employment status: “Which best describes your current work situation?” assessed with six response options: 0 = Unemployed, 1 = Full time learner/student, 2 = Studying and working, 3 = Occasional paid work, 4 = regular part-time paid work, 5 = regular full-time paid work
-> Recoded as 0 = unemployed (former option 0), 1 = employed/in education (former options 1 to 5)

- Subjective financial situation: “How would you describe the financial situation of your household?” rated with three response options: 1 = we have great difficulties, our financial situation is bad, 2 = sometimes we have slight difficulties, but our situation is average, and 3 = we do not have any financial problems, our financial situation is good
-> Recoded as 0 = bad (former option 1), 1 = not bad (former options 2 and 3)
table.indices: We will reverse code items of all multi-item measures (e.g., life satisfaction, personality traits) if necessary and calculate a mean score for the analyses. Furthermore, we will recode categorical variables as described above.
table.statistical_tests:
All analyses will be conducted in R. Our analyses will comprise two parts. In Part 1, we will examine personality-outcome associations using longitudinal correlations to obtain effect size estimates that can be compared with findings from Western countries. In Part 2, we will use specification curve analyses as implemented in package specr to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations across various analytical decisions (Masur & Scharkow, 2020). 

Part 1: Longitudinal Correlations

We will calculate longitudinal correlations between personality traits assessed at W1 (or W3 if W1 was missing) and life outcomes assessed at W7. We will use Person correlations for metric life outcomes (e.g., subjective well-being) and point-biserial correlations for binary life outcomes (e.g., employment status).

For these analyses, we will focus on the size of correlations and compare these effect sizes to findings from Western countries (see Table 1).

Part 2: Specification Curve Analysis

Specification curve analysis allows us to examine the consistency of results across a broad range of possible model specifications. With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are estimated, and then the robustness of effects across different model specifications is tested systematically (Simonsohn et al., 2020). 

We will estimate one specification curve for each trait-outcome combination (i.e., 14 specification curves in total). Life outcomes assessed at W7 will serve as dependent variables. Personality traits assessed at W1 will serve as predictors. We will either use linear or logistic regression models for the specification curve analyses, depending on whether the dependent variable is metric or binary. Specification curve analysis comprises three steps.

Step 1: Identification of All Specifications of Interest

As a first step, we will identify all reasonable ways to specify our regression models. In our case, we will estimate models with different covariates, predictors, outcomes, and (sub)samples. We will examine 128 different model specifications for each trait-outcome combination.

Analytical Decision 1: Covariates (Age, Gender, Education, Family Affluence)
Demographic characteristics like age, gender, family affluence, and education may confound the association between personality traits and important life outcomes. Similar to the approach of Beck and Jackson (2022), we will test whether personality-outcome relations are consistent across models with/without different covariates.
To assess family affluence, we will use four items from the Family Affluence Scale II (Boyce et al., 2006; Rotzinger et al., 2024).

Analytical Decision 2: Sample (Overall, Namibian subsample, Kenyan subsample, South African subsample)
The ALLS comprises individuals living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three countries. We will thus test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across the three subsamples and in the overall sample.

Analytical Decision 3: Different Ways to Estimate Personality Traits (Latent, Manifest)
In existing research, personality-outcome associations are typically examined using manifest variables (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023). However, other research topics, for example, personality trait changes, are often addressed using latent variables (Borghuis et al., 2017; Brandt et al., 2023; Haehner et al., 2025). As some of the personality traits included in this study have been found to have relatively low internal consistencies, using latent variables may also be beneficial to examine personality-outcome associations in our sample. Thus, we will test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across manifest and latent ways to score personality traits.
Specifically, to create latent personality trait scores, we will use the predicted factor scores from structural equation models. We will estimate one structural equation model for each personality trait using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012). We will use the indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood estimation to estimate these models. We will estimate partially invariant measurement models across countries, as done by Haehner et al. (2025) for the Big Two personality traits.

Analytical Decision 4: Using W1 or W3 Personality Data
We will either use W1 or W3 personality data to examine personality outcome associations because W1 personality data allows us to examine a longer retest interval (i.e., 3 years), whereas using W3 personality data will lead to a higher sample size.

Step 2: Descriptive Specification Curve

In a second step, we will estimate all possible model specifications identified in Step 1. We will then depict the result in a descriptive specification curve, which illustrates the effect size of interest – ranked from lowest/most negative to highest/most positive – along with the corresponding model specifications. For metric outcomes, we will depict standardized regression coefficients. For binary outcomes, we will depict Odds Ratios. 
Furthermore, we will examine and visualize which analytical decisions mattered the most for the effect size of interest (e.g., how much variance a specific analytical decision explain in the effect sizes).

Step 3: Joint Statistical Tests

In a third step, we will calculate joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications speaks against the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable (Simonsohn et al., 2020). 
For these joint statistical tests, we will use the permutation test technique similar to the procedure of Beck and Jackson (2022), Haehner et al. (2024), and Rohrer (2017). With the premutation test technique, we first create a dataset under the null hypotheses (i.e., no association) by shuffling the values of personality traits across people. In this dataset, we estimate all model specifications. We will then repeat Step 1 and Step 2, 500 times to generate a distribution of specification curves under the null hypotheses. Finally, we will use this distribution to conduct two statistical tests (Simonsohn et al., 2020): 
- We will estimate the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compare it to the observed median effect size in the specification curve of the original sample
- We will compute the average p value in each specification curve under the null (transformed to the z values using Stouffer’s method) and compare it with the average observed p value in the specification curve of the original sample

We will interpret findings as providing consistent evidence for a personality-outcome association if both statistical test lead to the same conclusion.
table.transformations: We will standardize all metric variables.
table.inference_criteria: We will use a level of significance of α = .05 for all analyses. Furthermore, we will compare effect sizes (and their 95% confidence intervals) across traits and outcomes as well as to findings from Western countries.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude data from assessment waves where participants failed the attention check items (e.g., “For this item, please tick the box for slightly inaccurate”). Specifically, at W1, we will only exclude participants if they failed all attention check items (as some participants did not seem to understand this type of attention check items). At other waves, where an improved quality check items were used, we will exclude participants who  failed at least two attention check items.
table.missing_data_handling: All cases with data for the dependent and independent variables will be included in the analyses.

table.title: Personality-Outcome Links in Sub-Saharan Africa
table.research_questions:
Although there are reasons to believe that findings from Western countries might not generalize to the three sub-Saharan countries (Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa), the existing research nonetheless serves as a useful starting point for the formulation of hypotheses. Table 1 provides an overview of findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries. Furthermore, we also included one longitudinal study on personality-outcome associations that was conducted in sub-Saharan Africa in this table (Kura et al., 2025).

Based on this existing evidence and the conceptual overlap of different personality taxonomies, we then developed hypotheses for the present study (see Table 2). Specifically, Extraversion, Openness, and low negative emotions (Emotional Stability) are components of Agency, while Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and even-temper (Emotional Stability) are components of Communion (Thalmayer, Mather, et al., 2024). 

(Table 1 and 2 have been uploaded as separate files to the Design plan section of this preregistration to ensure readability)
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will use data from Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer, Asatsa, et al., 2024), an ongoing longitudinal study conducted in sub-Saharan Africa with surveys every 6 months. For this study, we will use data from W1 to W7, which have been collected between January 2022 and April 2025.

ALLS was addressed to young adults (aged 18 to 21) from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Eligible individuals were identified with the help from local research assistants who recruited potential participants via local networks, community events, and high schools. After providing written informed consent, participants completed the surveys of the different assessment waves on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants’ devices, or on paper. Each wave comprised questionnaires about participants’ personality traits, well-being, mental health, and demographic variables. All questionnaires were provided in English. More details about the study design of the ALLS can be found in Thalmayer, Asata, et al. (2024).

For the present study, we will use data on the Big Two personality traits collected at W1 and W3 and data on life outcomes collected at W7. 68188ba7aceb5a48ea5ef82d Tables_Preregistration.pdf https://osf.io/project/5zw4a/files/osfstorage/68188ba7aceb5a48ea5ef82d https://osf.io/download/68188ba7aceb5a48ea5ef82d 1c0a25894fbb700b2a379b3a73cb051d8531b82fcb5857f7e41c782ec8090667
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: Data from the ALLS have been used in three previous publications (Haehner et al., 2025; Kura et al., 2025; Thalmayer, Mather, et al., 2024). These publications examined the structure, correlates, and changes of personality traits in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Furthermore, one study also examined longitudinal correlations between Big Six personality traits and anxiety, depression, and mental health at W5 (Kura et al., 2025). Thus, there are initial insights on personality-outcome associations for some traits and outcomes. However, the study by Kura and colleagues (2025) used a different personality inventory, different assessment waves and a different statistical approach compared to the ones used here. Specifically, data from W7 has only recently been collected and has not been analyzed before.
table.data_collection_procedures:
ALLS included participants (a) living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, (b) aged between 18 and 21 years at W1, and (c) speaking basic English. 
Participants were recruited from rural villages, towns and urban areas, including from informal settlements. Local research assistants reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools. 
The study used a combination of online and paper-pencil methods for data collection. Many participants had to be re-contacted in person via the local research assistants for each assessment wave. This procedure allowed to collect a more representative sample compared to online-only studies as internet access varies across the three countries.
To compensate for dropout, booster samples were added to the study at W3 following the same data collection procedures.
table.sample_size:
Overall, 3’048 individuals took part in W1 of the ALLS. However, 700 individuals could not be reached again at W2 and a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3.
For the present study, we will restrict the sample to individuals who took part in either W1 or W3 and W7. Furthermore, we will exclude data from measurement occasions where participants failed to pass attention check items. The final sample size for our analyses thus still has to be determined.
table.sample_size_rationale: We expect a final sample size of approximately N = 1800 individuals. With this sample size and a level of significance of 5%, we will have a power of 93% to detect a small effect of a personality-outcome association (i.e., corresponding to an effect size of R2 = 1%).
table.stopping_rule: Not applicable as data has already been collected.
table.measured_variables:
Big Two personality traits (assessed at W1 and W3): assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory (Thalmayer, Mather, et al., 2024): The 45 Items (e.g., “I tend to be calm”) were assessed on a 6-point response scale ranging from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate)

Life outcomes (assessed at W7):

- Subjective well-being assessed with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985): Three items (e.g., “I am satisfied with my life”) were assessed on a 7-point response scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree)

- Self-reported health: “In general, would you say your health is...” rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent)

- Depression and anxiety assessed with the depression and anxiety subscales of the International Mental Health Assessment (Thalmayer et al., 2023): Items (e.g., “I felt scared” were assessed on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (not in the last month/never) to 7 (daily)

- Relationship status: “Are you in a romantic relationship?” assessed with five response options: 0 = I am not in a relationship, 1 = I am in a relationship but do not live with my partner, 2 = I am in a relationship and live with my partner, 3 = I am married, 4 = Other
-> Recoded as 0 = no relationship (former option 0), 1 = in relationship (former options 1 to 3)

- Employment status: “Which best describes your current work situation?” assessed with six response options: 0 = Unemployed, 1 = Full time learner/student, 2 = Studying and working, 3 = Occasional paid work, 4 = regular part-time paid work, 5 = regular full-time paid work
-> Recoded as 0 = unemployed (former option 0), 1 = employed/in education (former options 1 to 5)

- Subjective financial situation: “How would you describe the financial situation of your household?” rated with three response options: 1 = we have great difficulties, our financial situation is bad, 2 = sometimes we have slight difficulties, but our situation is average, and 3 = we do not have any financial problems, our financial situation is good
-> Recoded as 0 = bad (former option 1), 1 = not bad (former options 2 and 3)
table.indices: We will reverse code items of all multi-item measures (e.g., life satisfaction, personality traits) if necessary and calculate a mean score for the analyses. Furthermore, we will recode categorical variables as described above.
table.statistical_tests:
All analyses will be conducted in R. Our analyses will comprise two parts. In Part 1, we will examine personality-outcome associations using longitudinal correlations to obtain effect size estimates that can be compared with findings from Western countries. In Part 2, we will use specification curve analyses as implemented in package specr to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations across various analytical decisions (Masur & Scharkow, 2020). 

Part 1: Longitudinal Correlations

We will calculate longitudinal correlations between personality traits assessed at W1 (or W3 if W1 was missing) and life outcomes assessed at W7. We will use Person correlations for metric life outcomes (e.g., subjective well-being) and point-biserial correlations for binary life outcomes (e.g., employment status).

For these analyses, we will focus on the size of correlations and compare these effect sizes to findings from Western countries (see Table 1).

Part 2: Specification Curve Analysis

Specification curve analysis allows us to examine the consistency of results across a broad range of possible model specifications. With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are estimated, and then the robustness of effects across different model specifications is tested systematically (Simonsohn et al., 2020). 

We will estimate one specification curve for each trait-outcome combination (i.e., 14 specification curves in total). Life outcomes assessed at W7 will serve as dependent variables. Personality traits assessed at W1 will serve as predictors. We will either use linear or logistic regression models for the specification curve analyses, depending on whether the dependent variable is metric or binary. Specification curve analysis comprises three steps.

Step 1: Identification of All Specifications of Interest

As a first step, we will identify all reasonable ways to specify our regression models. In our case, we will estimate models with different covariates, predictors, outcomes, and (sub)samples. We will examine 128 different model specifications for each trait-outcome combination.

Analytical Decision 1: Covariates (Age, Gender, Education, Family Affluence)
Demographic characteristics like age, gender, family affluence, and education may confound the association between personality traits and important life outcomes. Similar to the approach of Beck and Jackson (2022), we will test whether personality-outcome relations are consistent across models with/without different covariates.
To assess family affluence, we will use four items from the Family Affluence Scale II (Boyce et al., 2006; Rotzinger et al., 2024).

Analytical Decision 2: Sample (Overall, Namibian subsample, Kenyan subsample, South African subsample)
The ALLS comprises individuals living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three countries. We will thus test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across the three subsamples and in the overall sample.

Analytical Decision 3: Different Ways to Estimate Personality Traits (Latent, Manifest)
In existing research, personality-outcome associations are typically examined using manifest variables (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023). However, other research topics, for example, personality trait changes, are often addressed using latent variables (Borghuis et al., 2017; Brandt et al., 2023; Haehner et al., 2025). As some of the personality traits included in this study have been found to have relatively low internal consistencies, using latent variables may also be beneficial to examine personality-outcome associations in our sample. Thus, we will test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across manifest and latent ways to score personality traits.
Specifically, to create latent personality trait scores, we will use the predicted factor scores from structural equation models. We will estimate one structural equation model for each personality trait using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012). We will use the indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood estimation to estimate these models. We will estimate partially invariant measurement models across countries, as done by Haehner et al. (2025) for the Big Two personality traits.

Analytical Decision 4: Using W1 or W3 Personality Data
We will either use W1 or W3 personality data to examine personality outcome associations because W1 personality data allows us to examine a longer retest interval (i.e., 3 years), whereas using W3 personality data will lead to a higher sample size.

Step 2: Descriptive Specification Curve

In a second step, we will estimate all possible model specifications identified in Step 1. We will then depict the result in a descriptive specification curve, which illustrates the effect size of interest – ranked from lowest/most negative to highest/most positive – along with the corresponding model specifications. For metric outcomes, we will depict standardized regression coefficients. For binary outcomes, we will depict Odds Ratios. 
Furthermore, we will examine and visualize which analytical decisions mattered the most for the effect size of interest (e.g., how much variance a specific analytical decision explain in the effect sizes).

Step 3: Joint Statistical Tests

In a third step, we will calculate joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications speaks against the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable (Simonsohn et al., 2020). 
For these joint statistical tests, we will use the permutation test technique similar to the procedure of Beck and Jackson (2022), Haehner et al. (2024), and Rohrer (2017). With the premutation test technique, we first create a dataset under the null hypotheses (i.e., no association) by shuffling the values of personality traits across people. In this dataset, we estimate all model specifications. We will then repeat Step 1 and Step 2, 500 times to generate a distribution of specification curves under the null hypotheses. Finally, we will use this distribution to conduct two statistical tests (Simonsohn et al., 2020): 
- We will estimate the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compare it to the observed median effect size in the specification curve of the original sample
- We will compute the average p value in each specification curve under the null (transformed to the z values using Stouffer’s method) and compare it with the average observed p value in the specification curve of the original sample

We will interpret findings as providing consistent evidence for a personality-outcome association if both statistical test lead to the same conclusion.
table.transformations: We will standardize all metric variables.
table.inference_criteria: We will use a level of significance of α = .05 for all analyses. Furthermore, we will compare effect sizes (and their 95% confidence intervals) across traits and outcomes as well as to findings from Western countries.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude data from assessment waves where participants failed the attention check items (e.g., “For this item, please tick the box for slightly inaccurate”). Specifically, at W1, we will only exclude participants if they failed all attention check items (as some participants did not seem to understand this type of attention check items). At other waves, where an improved quality check items were used, we will exclude participants who  failed at least two attention check items.
table.missing_data_handling: All cases with data for the dependent and independent variables will be included in the analyses.

Furthermore, we will recode categorical variables as described above.", "All analyses will be conducted in R. Our analyses will comprise two parts. In Part 1, we will examine personality-outcome associations using longitudinal correlations to obtain effect size estimates that can be compared with findings from Western countries. In Part 2, we will use specification curve analyses as implemented in package specr to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations across various analytical decisions (Masur & Scharkow, 2020).

Part 1: Longitudinal Correlations

We will calculate longitudinal correlations between personality traits assessed at W1 (or W3 if W1 was missing) and life outcomes assessed at W7. We will use Person correlations for metric life outcomes (e.g., subjective well-being) and point-biserial correlations for binary life outcomes (e.g., employment status).

For these analyses, we will focus on the size of correlations and compare these effect sizes to findings from Western countries (see Table 1).

Part 2: Specification Curve Analysis

Specification curve analysis allows us to examine the consistency of results across a broad range of possible model specifications. With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are estimated, and then the robustness of effects across different model specifications is tested systematically (Simonsohn et al., 2020).

We will estimate one specification curve for each trait-outcome combination (i.e., 14 specification curves in total). Life outcomes assessed at W7 will serve as dependent variables. Personality traits assessed at W1 will serve as predictors. We will either use linear or logistic regression models for the specification curve analyses, depending on whether the dependent variable is metric or binary. Specification curve analysis comprises three steps.

Step 1: Identification of All Specifications of Interest

As a first step, we will identify all reasonable ways to specify our regression models. In our case, we will estimate models with different covariates, predictors, outcomes, and (sub)samples. We will examine 128 different model specifications for each trait-outcome combination.

Analytical Decision 1: Covariates (Age, Gender, Education, Family Affluence)
Demographic characteristics like age, gender, family affluence, and education may confound the association between personality traits and important life outcomes. Similar to the approach of Beck and Jackson (2022), we will test whether personality-outcome relations are consistent across models with/without different covariates.
To assess family affluence, we will use four items from the Family Affluence Scale II (Boyce et al., 2006; Rotzinger et al., 2024).

Analytical Decision 2: Sample (Overall, Namibian subsample, Kenyan subsample, South African subsample)
The ALLS comprises individuals living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three countries. We will thus test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across the three subsamples and in the overall sample.

Analytical Decision 3: Different Ways to Estimate Personality Traits (Latent, Manifest)
In existing research, personality-outcome associations are typically examined using manifest variables (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023). However, other research topics, for example, personality trait changes, are often addressed using latent variables (Borghuis et al., 2017; Brandt et al., 2023; Haehner et al., 2025). As some of the personality traits included in this study have been found to have relatively low internal consistencies, using latent variables may also be beneficial to examine personality-outcome associations in our sample. Thus, we will test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across manifest and latent ways to score personality traits.
Specifically, to create latent personality trait scores, we will use the predicted factor scores from structural equation models. We will estimate one structural equation model for each personality trait using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012). We will use the indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood estimation to estimate these models. We will estimate partially invariant measurement models across countries, as done by Haehner et al. (2025) for the Big Two personality traits.

Analytical Decision 4: Using W1 or W3 Personality Data
We will either use W1 or W3 personality data to examine personality outcome associations because W1 personality data allows us to examine a longer retest interval (i.e., 3 years), whereas using W3 personality data will lead to a higher sample size.

Step 2: Descriptive Specification Curve

In a second step, we will estimate all possible model specifications identified in Step 1. We will then depict the result in a descriptive specification curve, which illustrates the effect size of interest – ranked from lowest/most negative to highest/most positive – along with the corresponding model specifications. For metric outcomes, we will depict standardized regression coefficients. For binary outcomes, we will depict Odds Ratios.
Furthermore, we will examine and visualize which analytical decisions mattered the most for the effect size of interest (e.g., how much variance a specific analytical decision explain in the effect sizes).

Step 3: Joint Statistical Tests

In a third step, we will calculate joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications speaks against the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable (Simonsohn et al., 2020).
For these joint statistical tests, we will use the permutation test technique similar to the procedure of Beck and Jackson (2022), Haehner et al. (2024), and Rohrer (2017). With the premutation test technique, we first create a dataset under the null hypotheses (i.e., no association) by shuffling the values of personality traits across people. In this dataset, we estimate all model specifications. We will then repeat Step 1 and Step 2, 500 times to generate a distribution of specification curves under the null hypotheses. Finally, we will use this distribution to conduct two statistical tests (Simonsohn et al., 2020):
- We will estimate the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compare it to the observed median effect size in the specification curve of the original sample
- We will compute the average p value in each specification curve under the null (transformed to the z values using Stouffer’s method) and compare it with the average observed p value in the specification curve of the original sample

Part 1: Longitudinal Correlations

We will calculate longitudinal correlations between personality traits assessed at W1 (or W3 if W1 was missing) and life outcomes assessed at W7. We will use Person correlations for metric life outcomes (e.g., subjective well-being) and point-biserial correlations for binary life outcomes (e.g., employment status).

Part 2: Specification Curve Analysis

Specification curve analysis allows us to examine the consistency of results across a broad range of possible model specifications. With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are estimated, and then the robustness of effects across different model specifications is tested systematically (Simonsohn et al., 2020).

We will estimate one specification curve for each trait-outcome combination (i.e., 14 specification curves in total). Life outcomes assessed at W7 will serve as dependent variables. Personality traits assessed at W1 will serve as predictors. We will either use linear or logistic regression models for the specification curve analyses, depending on whether the dependent variable is metric or binary. Specification curve analysis comprises three steps.

Step 1: Identification of All Specifications of Interest

As a first step, we will identify all reasonable ways to specify our regression models. In our case, we will estimate models with different covariates, predictors, outcomes, and (sub)samples. We will examine 128 different model specifications for each trait-outcome combination.

Analytical Decision 1: Covariates (Age, Gender, Education, Family Affluence)
Demographic characteristics like age, gender, family affluence, and education may confound the association between personality traits and important life outcomes. Similar to the approach of Beck and Jackson (2022), we will test whether personality-outcome relations are consistent across models with/without different covariates.
To assess family affluence, we will use four items from the Family Affluence Scale II (Boyce et al., 2006; Rotzinger et al., 2024).

Analytical Decision 2: Sample (Overall, Namibian subsample, Kenyan subsample, South African subsample)
The ALLS comprises individuals living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three countries. We will thus test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across the three subsamples and in the overall sample.

Analytical Decision 3: Different Ways to Estimate Personality Traits (Latent, Manifest)
In existing research, personality-outcome associations are typically examined using manifest variables (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023). However, other research topics, for example, personality trait changes, are often addressed using latent variables (Borghuis et al., 2017; Brandt et al., 2023; Haehner et al., 2025). As some of the personality traits included in this study have been found to have relatively low internal consistencies, using latent variables may also be beneficial to examine personality-outcome associations in our sample. Thus, we will test the consistency of personality-outcome relations across manifest and latent ways to score personality traits.
Specifically, to create latent personality trait scores, we will use the predicted factor scores from structural equation models. We will estimate one structural equation model for each personality trait using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012). We will use the indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood estimation to estimate these models. We will estimate partially invariant measurement models across countries, as done by Haehner et al. (2025) for the Big Two personality traits.

Analytical Decision 4: Using W1 or W3 Personality Data
We will either use W1 or W3 personality data to examine personality outcome associations because W1 personality data allows us to examine a longer retest interval (i.e., 3 years), whereas using W3 personality data will lead to a higher sample size.

Step 2: Descriptive Specification Curve

In a second step, we will estimate all possible model specifications identified in Step 1. We will then depict the result in a descriptive specification curve, which illustrates the effect size of interest – ranked from lowest/most negative to highest/most positive – along with the corresponding model specifications. For metric outcomes, we will depict standardized regression coefficients. For binary outcomes, we will depict Odds Ratios.
Furthermore, we will examine and visualize which analytical decisions mattered the most for the effect size of interest (e.g., how much variance a specific analytical decision explain in the effect sizes).

Step 3: Joint Statistical Tests

In a third step, we will calculate joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications speaks against the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable (Simonsohn et al., 2020).
For these joint statistical tests, we will use the permutation test technique similar to the procedure of Beck and Jackson (2022), Haehner et al. (2024), and Rohrer (2017). With the premutation test technique, we first create a dataset under the null hypotheses (i.e., no association) by shuffling the values of personality traits across people. In this dataset, we estimate all model specifications. We will then repeat Step 1 and Step 2, 500 times to generate a distribution of specification curves under the null hypotheses. Finally, we will use this distribution to conduct two statistical tests (Simonsohn et al., 2020):
- We will estimate the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compare it to the observed median effect size in the specification curve of the original sample

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 1419 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  16 of 736 data columns (2%) are documented in a codebook; 720 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (1419 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 2% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `Scale`, `Admin`, `Demographics` while the data has `id`, `country`, `age`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 736 data columns across 2 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (1419 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 2% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `Scale`, `Admin`, `Demographics` while the data has `id`, `country`, `age`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: ALLS participants are young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, mainly aged 18, but up to age 21, at W1.
They were recruited by local research assistants who found eligible individuals at schools, church groups, and community events.

To take part in the study, participants provided written informed consent, then they completed the first survey either on an electronic tablet carried by a research assistant, on paper, or via a link sent to participant's device.

Participants were recontacted for subsequent waves either online or in-person via local research assistants, which allowed for a more representative sample compared to an online-only study in these contexts.
At W1, 3,048 young adults were recruited to participate in ALLS.
Participants were, on average, 18.32 years old (SD = 0.76), with 58% reporting having completed high school and 36% reported to be looking for employment.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

"01 Data Preparation.R", "02 Specification Curve Analyses.R",

"02 Specification Curve Analyses.R"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", 
"dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `Data/data_scored.RData` to `data_scored.RData` (in 02 Specification Curve Analyses.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `w1w7_anon.csv`.
#### Files not run on their own
1 file only defines functions, so running it on its own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}

-1L), class = "data.frame")

metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. text.text: Africa played a key role in the ALLS data collection, which would not have been possible without their dedicated efforts, especially their direct engagement with participants throughout the process.
We would therefore like to thank all those who contributed to this data collection.
We have no conflicts of interest to report.
Research goal: Personality traits describe how we think, feel, and behave.
More agentic people, for example, tend to be more confident, sociable, and fearless, whereas more communal people are more respectful, moral, warm, and even-tempered.
Research has shown that personality traits such as agency and communion predict life outcomes such as health, well-being, and employment.
However, the evidence for this comes almost exclusively from Western countries.
We tested whether the links between personality traits and important life outcomes replicate in African contexts and whether these links are robust across different ways to analyze the data.

Methods: Using a sample of young adults from Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa (N = 2,770), we examined how personality traits are related to life outcomes like health, employment, and depression over 2 to 3 years.
We found that more agentic and more communal people tended to have higher levels of self-rated health and lower levels of anxiety and depression.
Being more communal also predicted being employed 2 to 3 years later.
However, the associations were smaller than in Western countries and depended on factors such as the time lag between assessments.
Our findings provide important insights into how links between personality traits and life outcomes differ across cultural contexts.

Personality traits -characteristic patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors -have been found to predict outcomes across important life domains, including educational attainment (Mammadov, 2022; Noftle & Robins, 2007), relationship success (Wagner et al., 2015), income (Denissen et al., 2018), health (Jokela et al., 2018; Kern & Friedman, 2011), the occurrence of major life stressors (Santee et al., 2023), and mortality (Jokela et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2007).

text.text: Furthermore, personality-outcome links have been replicated across samples, a range of possible covariates, and research methods (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023), underlining the robustness of personality-outcome associations (Bleidorn et al., 2019).

text.text: Findings on the predictive power of personality traits, however, stem almost exclusively from Western countries, home to only 11% of the world's population (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division, 2024).

text.text: Although a handful of studies have tested personality-outcome associations in African countries, these were typically limited by small samples, non-validated personality inventories, and/or cross-sectional designs (Du Preez et al., 2011; Kinyanjui & Sum, 2023; Nel et al., 2017; Papenfus et al., 2024; Peltzer, 2002).

text.text: These limitations leave unclear whether findings on personality-outcome associations generalize to African countries.

As virtually all psychological phenomena are impacted by cultural context, it cannot be assumed that findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries generalize to all people (Henrich et al., 2010; Kitayama & Salvador, 2024).

text.text: With the present study, we address the cross-cultural generalizability of personalityoutcome links.

To do so, we use longitudinal data from the Africa Long Life Study (Thalmayer et al., 2024), which, as of 2025, had assessed personality traits and life outcomes over 3 years among young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa.
text.formatted: To do so, we use longitudinal data from the Africa Long Life Study <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Thalmayer et al., 2024)</ref>, which, as of 2025, had assessed personality traits and life outcomes over 3 years among young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa.

text.text: We examine longitudinal associations between personality traits and seven important life outcomes: self-reported health, subjective well-being, depression, anxiety, relationship status, employment status, and subjective financial status.
Furthermore, we use specification curve analyses to investigate the robustness of these associations across various analytic decisions such as covariates or country.

Over the last decades, robust predictive links between personality traits and various important life outcomes have been identified, highlighting the practical and societal relevance of personality traits (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Bleidorn et al., 2019; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023).

text.text: Most studies on this topic focused on the Big Five personality traitsagreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, emotional stability, and opennessand examined outcomes across life domains such as well-being, health, work, and relationships (Bleidorn, 2024; Bleidorn et al., 2019).

text.text: For example, there is consistent evidence that higher levels of conscientiousness and extraversion predict better health status several years later, whereas higher levels of neuroticism have consistently been linked to mental health problems like depression and anxiety (Kotov et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2022; Turiano et al., 2012; Wright & Jackson, 2023).

text.text: The size of personality-outcome links differs across outcomes and studies, but most studies found at least medium-sized associations of r = .20 (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Roberts et al., 2007).

text.text: These findings appear to provide a solid knowledge basis regarding the predictive power of personality traits.
However, it is unclear whether these personality-outcome associations can be replicated in non-Western countries.

Investigating these effects in sub-Saharan Africa is of importance because this region provides a meaningful cultural contrast to Western contexts in various socio-cultural and ecological respects, making for a compelling test of cross-cultural replicability of current theories.

It is also home to more of the world's population than all Western countries combined (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division, 2024), making the predictive utility of personality trait measures an important practical question.
There are several reasons to anticipate that findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries might not generalize to sub-Saharan Africa.
First, the most important personality traits and their structure differ in African compared to Western societies (Thalmayer et al., 2020 (Thalmayer et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: First, the most important personality traits and their structure differ in African compared to Western societies <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Thalmayer et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Thalmayer et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: While most research in Western countries has focused on the Big Five personality traits (Bleidorn, 2024), it has recently been shown that the Big Two personality traits, agency and communion, may work better for cross-cultural comparisons in personality research (Thalmayer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: While most research in Western countries has focused on the Big Five personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>, it has recently been shown that the Big Two personality traits, agency and communion, may work better for cross-cultural comparisons in personality research <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Thalmayer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Agency describes the tendency to be confident, sociable, fearless, surgent, and positive, akin to the Big Five traits extraversion, openness, and low negative emotions (emotional stability).
Communion describes the tendency to be warm, respectful, moral, diligent, and even-tempered, akin to the Big Five traits agreeableness, conscientiousness, and even-temper (emotional stability).

Second, cultural contexts differ in what kind of behaviors are considered appropriate or desirable, and thus are rewarded or punished, which likely influences personality-outcome associations (Hofstede, 2011; Leung & Cohen, 2011).
text.formatted: Second, cultural contexts differ in what kind of behaviors are considered appropriate or desirable, and thus are rewarded or punished, which likely influences personality-outcome associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hofstede, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Leung & Cohen, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, individuals living in low-andmiddle-income countries, including those in sub-Saharan Africa, are faced with a greater degree of contextual challenges, including social, economic, and political risks (Herrero Romero et al., 2018; Uskul et al., 2024), making them more likely to experience poverty, crime, and domestic violence (Gradín, 2019; Theron et al., 2022).

text.text: These challenging conditions may influence the kind of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that are adaptive and thus influence personalityoutcome associations.

Third, there is evidence that young adults living in sub-Saharan Africa report different kinds of life events and differ in their personality-event transactions compared to young adults from Western countries, indicating that the interplay between personality traits and the environment may differ across cultural contexts (Haehner et al., 2026).

text.text: In sum, although there is robust evidence on personality-outcome associations in Western societies, it is unclear whether these findings generalize to sub-Saharan Africa.

Only a few small and cross-sectional studies have linked personality traits to life outcomes such as mental health, well-being, and health behaviors in African samples (Du Preez et al., 2011; Kinyanjui & Sum, 2023; Papenfus et al., 2024; Peltzer, 2002).

text.text: One previous study provided initial insights into longitudinal personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa using data from the Africa Long Life Study (Kura et al., 2025).

text.text: This study investigated whether markers of HEXACO/Big Six personality traits were related to mental and physical health.
The authors found, for example, that higher levels of conscientiousness and openness predicted better self-reported health 2 years later.
However, this study did not examine outcomes from other life domains and did not use thein this cultural contextmore psychometrically-sound Cross-Cultural Big Two personality traits.
Furthermore, findings on personality-outcome associations differed across countries and assessment waves, highlighting the necessity to test their robustness.
It is thus a first goal of the present study to examine longitudinal personality-outcome associations in three sub-Saharan countries and to compare results to those from Western countries.

Although personality-outcome links have been replicated across samples and research methods in Western countries, their robustness in non-Western countries has yet to be established (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019).

text.text: Only if personality-outcome links are robust, will they have practical relevance in the region, for example, in appropriately informing public health interventions (Bleidorn et al., 2019; Haehner, Wright, et al., 2024; Wright et al., 2026).

text.text: However, several analytic decisions, like the covariates included or the time interval between assessments, can influence the results on personality-outcome associations.
For instance, Beck and Jackson (2022) have shown that the predictive link between conscientiousness and employment status depends on age.

text.text: Thus, the second goal of the present study is to examine the robustness of personalityoutcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa.

To do so, we use specification curve analysis as a pragmatic way to test the relevance of different analytic decisions and to integrate a large number of results (similar to the approach of Beck & Jackson, 2022).
text.formatted: To do so, we use specification curve analysis as a pragmatic way to test the relevance of different analytic decisions and to integrate a large number of results (similar to the approach of <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beck & Jackson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: With specification curve analysis, researchers first identify and estimate all reasonable ways to specify a statistical model (Simonsohn et al., 2020).
text.formatted: With specification curve analysis, researchers first identify and estimate all reasonable ways to specify a statistical model <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Simonsohn et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In our case, we test the robustness of personality-outcome associations across different covariates, countries, and ways of capturing personality trait scores.
We then conduct a joint statistical test to examine whether all possible specifications support or refute a significant personality-outcome association.
The present study tests longitudinal personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa.

To do so, we use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer et al., 2024), which has assessed personality traits and important life outcomes such as employment status, self-reported health, and subjective well-being in young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa since 2022, providing up to 3 years of data at this time.
text.formatted: To do so, we use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Thalmayer et al., 2024)</ref>, which has assessed personality traits and important life outcomes such as employment status, self-reported health, and subjective well-being in young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa since 2022, providing up to 3 years of data at this time.

text.text: Using these data, we address two research questions: (1) Which personality traits are associated with important life outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa and how do effect sizes compare to results from Western countries?
(2) How robust are personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa and which analytic decisions influence effect sizes?
As evidence on personality-outcome associations from sub-Saharan Africa is still limited, we relied mainly on findings from Western countries to derive hypotheses.

Based on the existing evidence on personality-outcome associations (see Table 1) and the conceptual overlap of the Big Two and Big Five taxonomies, we developed nine hypotheses for the present study (Table 2).
text.formatted: Based on the existing evidence on personality-outcome associations (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>) and the conceptual overlap of the Big Two and Big Five taxonomies, we developed nine hypotheses for the present study (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: These hypotheses may be seen as a useful starting point for a more thorough empirical investigation of personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa as they provide benchmarks for comparisons.
However, as described above, there are also several reasons why findings from Western countries might not generalize to Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa.

Thus, deviations from these hypotheses should not be interpreted as contradicting prior empirical evidence but rather as indications of potential cultural differences, underlining the necessity of cross-cultural research.

text.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
ALLS is an ongoing longitudinal study with assessment waves every 6 months.
For this study, we used data from Waves 1, 3, and 7 (henceforward called W1, W3, and W7), collected between 2022 and 2025.
ALLS participants are young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, mainly aged 18, but up to age 21, at W1.
They were recruited by local research assistants who found eligible individuals at schools, church groups, and community events.
To compensate for dropout, booster samples were added at W3 using the same data collection methods.

To take part in the study, participants provided written informed consent, then they completed the first survey either on an electronic tablet carried by a research assistant, on paper, or via a link sent to participant's device.
Each wave comprised questionnaires about personality traits, well-being, mental health, cultural mindset, and socio-demographic characteristics.
All surveys were in English.

Participants were recontacted for subsequent waves either online or in-person via local research assistants, which allowed for a more representative sample compared to an online-only study in these contexts.
More details about the design and measures of ALLS used can be found in Thalmayer and colleagues (2024).
text.formatted: More details about the design and measures of ALLS used can be found in <ref type="bibr">Thalmayer and colleagues (2024)</ref>.

text.text: At W1, 3,048 young adults were recruited to participate in ALLS.
At W2, approximately 700 participants dropped out of the study or could not be reached again so a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3.
For the present analyses, we restricted the sample to participants who took part in W7 and in either W1 or W3.
Furthermore, we excluded participants who failed to pass attention check items (e.g., "Which of the following is a building?", with response options house, tree, plane, cat, and book).
Applying these exclusion criteria led to a final sample of N = 2,770.
With this sample size, we had a sufficient power of 80% to detect very small personality-outcome associations of r = .053 (Champely, 2006; Funder & Ozer, 2019).
text.formatted: With this sample size, we had a sufficient power of 80% to detect very small personality-outcome associations of r = .053 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Champely, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Funder & Ozer, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: At W1, 55% of the sample identified as female.
Participants were, on average, 18.32 years old (SD = 0.76), with 58% reporting having completed high school and 36% reported to be looking for employment.

We calculated mean scores for the analyses (anxiety: α = .85, depression: α = .87).

with six response options:0 = unemployed,1 = full time learner/student,2 = studying and working,3 = occasional paid work,4 = regular part-time paid work,5 = regular full-time paid work.

rated with three response options:1 = we have great difficulties, our financial situation is bad,2 = sometimes we have slight difficulties, but our situation is average, and3 = we do not have any financial problems, our financial situation is good.

Data analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.3.2) using R packages specr (Masur & Scharkow, 2020) and lavaan (Rosseel, 2012).

text.text: We used a level of α = .05 for all analyses and standardized all metric variables.
Our analyses comprised two parts.
First, we examined personality-outcome associations using longitudinal correlations to obtain effect size estimates that can be compared to findings from Western countries.
Then, we used specification curve analyses to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations across different analytic decisions.
We calculated longitudinal correlations between personality traits assessed at W1 (n = 1,720 for agency and n = 1,714 for communion) and life outcomes assessed at W7.
If W1 personality data was not available, we used W3 personality trait scores (n = 572 for agency and n = 578 for communion).
We used Pearson correlations for metric life outcomes (e.g., life satisfaction) and point-biserial correlations for binary life outcomes (e.g., employment status).
We focused on the size of correlations and compared these effect sizes to findings from Western countries (see Table 1).
text.formatted: We focused on the size of correlations and compared these effect sizes to findings from Western countries (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Specification curve analysis allowed us to examine the consistency of results across a broad range of possible model specifications.

With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are first estimated, and then the robustness of effects across these specifications is tested systematically (Simonsohn et al., 2020).
text.formatted: With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are first estimated, and then the robustness of effects across these specifications is tested systematically <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Simonsohn et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We estimated one specification curve for each trait-outcome combination (i.e., 14 specification curves in total).
Life outcomes assessed at W7 served as dependent variables.
Personality traits assessed at W1 or W3 served as predictors.
We either used linear or logistic regression models for the specification curve analyses, depending on whether the dependent variable was metric or binary.
Specification curve analyses comprised three steps.
As a first step, we identified all reasonable ways to specify our regression models.
In our case, we estimated models with different covariates, (sub)samples, ways to calculate personality trait scores, and retest intervals.
In total, we examined 256 model specifications for each trait-outcome combination.
Demographic characteristics like age, gender, family affluence, and education may confound the association between personality traits and important life outcomes.
Similar to Beck and Jackson (2022), we examined whether personality-outcome relations were robust across models with different covariates.
text.formatted: Similar to <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beck and Jackson (2022)</ref>, we examined whether personality-outcome relations were robust across models with different covariates.

text.text: ALLS comprises individuals living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa.
Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three ALLS countries (Kura et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three ALLS countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kura et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We thus tested the consistency of personality-outcome associations across the three subsamples and in the overall sample.
In prior research, personality-outcome associations have typically been examined using manifest variables (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023).
text.formatted: In prior research, personality-outcome associations have typically been examined using manifest variables (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beck & Jackson, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Soto, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Wright & Jackson, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, latent variables help to account for measurement error.
We thus tested the consistency of personalityoutcome associations between manifest and latent trait score calculations.

To create latent personality trait scores, we used the predicted factor scores from unidimensional structural equation models as by Haehner et al. (2026). Haehner et al. (2026) tested different measurement models of the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory against each other by comparing models with and without removing certain items.

text.text: Here, we relied on the measurement models including all items to increase comparability with manifest scores even though they had mediocre fit (Agency W1: CFI = .81, RMSEA = .09, Communion W1: CFI = .90, RMSEA = .09).
These models were estimated using the indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood estimation.

More details about latent measurement models including correlations between latent and manifest personality trait scores can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7.
