text.text: We either used W1 or W3 personality data to examine personality-outcome associations.
W1 personality data allowed us to examine a longer retest interval (i.e., 3 years), whereas W3 personality data led to a larger sample size.
In the second step, we estimated all possible model specifications identified in Step 1.

We then depicted the result in a descriptive specification curve, which illustrates the effect size of interest -ranked from lowest/most negative to highest/most positive -along with the corresponding model specifications.
For metric outcomes, we focused on standardized regression coefficients.
For binary outcomes, we used odds ratios.
Furthermore, we examined and visualized which analytic decisions mattered the most for the effect size of interest.

In the third step, we calculated joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications counters the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable (Simonsohn et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In the third step, we calculated joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications counters the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Simonsohn et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For these joint statistical tests, we used the permutation-test technique similar to the procedures of Beck and Jackson (2022), Haehner et al. (2024), and Rohrer (2017).
text.formatted: For these joint statistical tests, we used the permutation-test technique similar to the procedures of Beck and Jackson (2022), <ref type="bibr">Haehner et al. (2024), and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rohrer (2017)</ref>.

text.text: With the permutation-test technique, we first created a dataset under the null hypothesis (i.e., no association).
We used two different approaches to achieve this goal: We either shuffled the values of personality traits across participants or we shuffled the values of life outcomes across participants.
In these datasets, we estimated all model specifications.
We then repeated the previous two steps 500 times to generate a distribution of specification curves under the null hypotheses.
Finally, we used this distribution to conduct two statistical tests (Simonsohn et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Finally, we used this distribution to conduct two statistical tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Simonsohn et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: First, we estimated the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compared it to the observed https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 specification curve of the original sample.
text.formatted: First, we estimated the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compared it to the observed <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7">median effect size in the</ref> specification curve of the original sample.

text.text: Second, we computed the average p value in each specification curve under the null (transformed to z values using Stouffer's method) and compared it with the average observed p value in the specification curve of the original sample.

text.text: Longitudinal personality-outcome correlations assessed over 2 to 3 years are illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Longitudinal personality-outcome correlations assessed over 2 to 3 years are illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>.

text.text: As can be seen in this figure, higher levels of agency predicted higher levels of life satisfaction (r = .05, 95% CI = [.00, .09]) and self-rated health (r = .07, 95% CI = [.03, .11]), lower levels of anxiety (r = -.08, 95% CI = [-.12, -.04]) and depression (r = -.11, 95% CI = [-.15, -.07]), being in a relationship (r = .04, 95% CI = [.00, .09]), and being employed (r = .05, 95% CI = [.01, .09]) 2 to 3 years later.

Similarly, higher levels of communion predicted higher levels of life satisfaction (r = .05, 95% CI = [.00, .09]), lower levels of anxiety (r = -.06.95% CI = [-.10, -.02]), and being employed (r = .06, 95% CI = [.02, .10]) 2 to 3 years later.
Although these correlations were statistically significant, they were small according to common effectsize guidelines (Funder & Ozer, 2019).
text.formatted: Although these correlations were statistically significant, they were small according to common effectsize guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Funder & Ozer, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Next, we estimated specification curves to examine the robustness of personalityoutcome associations across different analytic decisions.

Specifically, we tested whether personality-outcome associations were robust across different covariates, time intervals between assessments, countries, and ways to calculate personality trait scores, leading to 256 model specifications for each personality-outcome association.

Figure 2 illustrates the specification curve for one personality-outcome association (see Section 3 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 for all other specification curves).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref> illustrates the specification curve for one personality-outcome association (see Section 3 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7">Supplementary Materials</ref> for all other specification curves).

text.text: This specification curve shows how the predictive link between agency and self-rated health varied across model specifications.
About half of the 256 models showed a positive and statistically-significant association between agency and self-rated health.
Country and the way personality was scored seemed to be the most influential analytic decisions, with stronger personality-health links in South Africa and Kenya and for manifest scores of agency.
A similar pattern also emerged for other personality-outcome combinations.
Figure 3 illustrates how much of the observed differences in personality-outcome associations could be explained by certain analytic decisions.

text.text: As can be seen in this figure, effect sizes of personality-outcome associations depended the most on the country of data collection and on whether personality traits were calculated as manifest or latent variables whereas the covariates (e.g., age, gender, education, family affluence) explained little variance in personality-outcome associationsfoot_0 .

In contrast, there was no clear pattern of how the country of data collection was related to effect size estimates.

text.text: To test whether the whole set of specifications counters the null hypothesis that there is no association between a personality trait and a life outcome, we ran four different kinds of permutation tests (see Methods section for details).

If all four tests were statistically significant, we interpreted the results as indicating a robust personality-outcome https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 decision rule to infer robustness).
text.formatted: If all four tests were statistically significant, we interpreted the results as indicating a robust personality-outcome <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7">association (i.e., a   conservative</ref> decision rule to infer robustness).

text.text: These permutation tests compare the observed result pattern across specifications (e.g., the median effect size of a personality-outcome association across all 256 specifications; βMedian) to 500 hypothetical scenarios where there should be no effect.
The corresponding p values thus indicate whether the observed result pattern is more extreme than what would have been expected if there was no association.

As summarized in Table 4, higher levels of agency were robustly linked to higher levels of selfrated health (βMedian = 0.05, p < .001), lower levels of anxiety (βMedian = -0.08, p < .001), and lower levels of depression (βMedian = -0.06, p < .001).

text.text: Furthermore, higher levels of communion were robustly linked to higher levels of self-rated health (βMedian = 0.07, p < .001), lower levels of anxiety (βMedian = -0.04, p = .016), lower levels of depression (βMedian = -0.05, p < .001), and being employed (βMedian = 0.12, p < .001).

text.text: As such, results were in line with Hypothesis 3 (agency and self-rated health), Hypothesis 4 (agency and depression), Hypothesis 5 (communion and depression), Hypothesis 6 (agency and anxiety), and Hypothesis 7 (communion and anxiety).

However, we did not find robust evidence for Hypothesis 1 (agency and life satisfaction), Hypothesis 2 (communion and life satisfaction), Hypothesis 8 (communion and relationship status), or Hypothesis 9 (agency and employment status).
In a non-preregistered step, we additionally explored whether findings on employment status and subjective financial status depended on the scoring of these variables.
For example, for employment status, we compared three scorings: unemployed vs. employed/education (main analyses), unemployed vs. employed, and unemployed vs. education.

Replicating the results of our main analyses, communion was consistently related to not being unemployed but there were no robust links for other personality-outcome combinations (see Section 4 of https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 for details).

text.text: Agency and communion are two broad personality traits that capture individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and behaviors at a relatively high level of aggregation.

According to Thalmayer et al. (2025), agency comprises lower-order components of competence, confidence, fearlessness, positive mood, sociability, and surgency, while communion comprises components of even-temper, industriousness, morality, respect, and warmth.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Thalmayer et al. (2025)</ref>, agency comprises lower-order components of competence, confidence, fearlessness, positive mood, sociability, and surgency, while communion comprises components of even-temper, industriousness, morality, respect, and warmth.

text.text: In an exploratory analysis, we examined personality-outcome associations using these lower-order components instead of the manifest-latent distinction as the analytic decision (see Section 5 of the Supplementary Materials for details).
These analyses revealed some differences in personality-outcome associations among Big Two components, illustrating the value of examining associations at a finer-grained level (Figure 4).
text.formatted: These analyses revealed some differences in personality-outcome associations among Big Two components, illustrating the value of examining associations at a finer-grained level (Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>).

text.text: For example, the agency-health link was primarily attributable to competence, fearlessness, positive mood, and surgency.
Similarly, the link between employment status and communion seemed to depend on industriousness, morality, and warmth.
Despite these differences, most of the personality-outcome associations identified as robust in our main analyses replicated with Big Two components as predictors.

Components explained between 1% and 31% of the variance in effect size estimates, suggesting that differences between components are relevant for the size of personality-outcome associations but less important than country or time-lag differences.

In the present study, we tested the cross-cultural generalizability of personality-outcome associations by examining longitudinal links between personality traits and seven important life outcomes in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa.
Using specification curve analyses, we also tested the robustness of personality-outcome associations across analytic decisions (e.g., time lag between assessment, country of data collection).
We found that higher levels of agency and communion consistently predicted higher levels of self-rated health and lower levels of anxiety and depression over 2 to 3 years.
Additionally, higher levels of communion predicted being employed 2 to 3 years later.
Although robust, the effect sizes of these personality-outcome associations were small (.02 ≤ |r| ≤ .11).

Furthermore, some personality-outcome links that are well-established in Western countries, including personality predictors of life satisfaction and relationship status, did not replicate in our sub-Saharan samples.
Differences among countries, lower-order components of the Big Two, and ways to score personality traits partially explained heterogeneity in personality-outcome associations.
Here, we discuss similarities and differences between our findings and prior results from Western countries and explore possible reasons for the divergences.
Our results partly replicated findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries.

In line with our hypotheses, which were based on those prior findings (see Table 2), higher levels of agency and communion were associated with better self-reported mental and physical health (Kotov et al., 2010; Soto, 2019; Turiano et al., 2012; Wright & Jackson, 2023).
text.formatted: In line with our hypotheses, which were based on those prior findings (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>), higher levels of agency and communion were associated with better self-reported mental and physical health <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kotov et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Soto, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Turiano et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Wright & Jackson, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similar to personality-outcome associations in Western countries, these links were robust across a range of analytic decisions, such as different covariates (e.g., age, gender, education) and time lags between assessments (Beck & Jackson, 2022).
text.formatted: Similar to personality-outcome associations in Western countries, these links were robust across a range of analytic decisions, such as different covariates (e.g., age, gender, education) and time lags between assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Beck & Jackson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These similarities in personality-outcome associations across cultural contexts support the view that agency and communion may function as basic human traits, capturing "adaptive" characteristics across cultural contexts (Saucier et al., 2014).
text.formatted: These similarities in personality-outcome associations across cultural contexts support the view that agency and communion may function as basic human traits, capturing "adaptive" characteristics across cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Saucier et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Agency (akin to high extraversion, high openness, and low negative emotions) reflects a general tendency to be confident, sociable, positive and competent.
High levels of agency could lead to better mental and physical health through more active coping behaviors, greater stress resistance, and higher health literacy.
Communion (akin to high agreeableness, high conscientiousness, and being even-tempered) describes the tendency to be warm, moral, and diligent.

Higher levels of this trait could be linked to mental health through less risky behaviors, larger social support networks, and more consistent health behaviors (Friedman & Kern, 2014; Kern & Friedman, 2011).
text.formatted: Higher levels of this trait could be linked to mental health through less risky behaviors, larger social support networks, and more consistent health behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Friedman & Kern, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kern & Friedman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Providing some nuance to these conclusions, exploratory analyses indicated that personality-outcome associations differed among lower-order components of the Big Two.

For example, the link between employment status and communion was strongest for components of industriousness, morality, and warmth, suggesting that thoughts, feelings, and behaviors related to conscientiousness and agreeableness rather than emotional stability are most relevant for personality-work associations in sub-Saharan Africa.

Consistent with results from Western countries, these findings illustrate the value of moving beyond broad trait domains to better understand personality-outcome links (Mõttus, 2016; Stewart et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consistent with results from Western countries, these findings illustrate the value of moving beyond broad trait domains to better understand personality-outcome links <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Mõttus, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Stewart et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Personality-outcome associations in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa also differed in some ways from Western findings.
Perhaps the most striking difference was the overall lower level of personality-outcome associations, with zero-order correlations ranging from |r| = .02 to .11.

These findings diverge from results of Haehner et al. (2026) who used the same sample but found larger selection effects for self-reported important life events than typically observed in Western countries.
text.formatted: These findings diverge from results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Haehner et al. (2026)</ref> who used the same sample but found larger selection effects for self-reported important life events than typically observed in Western countries.

text.text: However, small associations between traits and mental health outcomes are in line with results by Kura and colleagues (2025) who also used the same sample but a different personality inventory.
text.formatted: However, small associations between traits and mental health outcomes are in line with results by <ref type="bibr">Kura and colleagues (2025)</ref> who also used the same sample but a different personality inventory.

text.text: There are several possible reasons for the small associations between personality traits and life outcomes.
Methodological factors like ceiling effects and restricted variance could be at play.

Young adults in our sample rated their trait levels relatively highly, with average values of 4.5 on a scale from 1 to 6 and with less variance than typically seen in Western samples (De Vries et al., 2021; Haehner et al., 2022), potentially limiting their predictive utility.
text.formatted: Young adults in our sample rated their trait levels relatively highly, with average values of 4.5 on a scale from 1 to 6 and with less variance than typically seen in Western samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(De Vries et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Haehner et al., 2022)</ref>, potentially limiting their predictive utility.

text.text: Methodological factors could also explain why associations differed between manifest and latent personality trait variables.

Latent personality-outcome associations might have been smaller because latent they had less variance in our sample (see Section 1 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7).
text.formatted: Latent personality-outcome associations might have been smaller because latent they had less variance in our sample (see Section 1 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7">Supplementary Materials</ref>).

text.text: Relatedly, latent and manifest personality scores were only moderately correlated in this sample, indicating that observed variance in personality traits was only partly explained by underlying similarities among the items.
This could be due to unreliability of the measure or problems with the measurement model, both of which could reduce personality-outcome associations.
To test the relevance of these methodological factors, future research comparing findings across personality measures would be needed.
A substantive possibility is that contextual factors are functionally more important for predicting life outcomes in African contexts, limiting the predictive power of traits.
Young adults in sub-Saharan Africa face interconnected societal challenges such as poverty, inequality, and high unemployment (Gradín, 2019; Theron et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Young adults in sub-Saharan Africa face interconnected societal challenges such as poverty, inequality, and high unemployment <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gradín, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Theron et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These challenges present structural barriers to achieving desired life outcomes, despite having high levels of agency and/or communion.
An indication supporting the relevance of contextual factors is the finding that country explained a large proportion of the effect size differences in specification curve analyses.
Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa differ in ways that could help explain differences in personality-outcome associations.

For example, the countries differ in youth unemployment rate (Kenya: 67%, South Africa: 46%, Namibia: 37%) and age of first marriage (Kenya: 25.6 years, Namibia: 29.2 years, South Africa: 31.0 years), potentially influencing personalityemployment and personality-relationship associations (Federation of Kenya Employers, 2024; South African Government, 2024; The World Bank, 2025; World Population Review, 2025).
It was not the case, however, such that one country always showed the strongest or weakest associations.
Thus, sampling differences are an alternative explanation for the country differences.
The South African sample included more university students recruits, whereas almost all Namibian and Kenyan recruits were high school students at Wave 1.
To tease these explanations apart, future research may need to replicate our findings in independent -and ideally representative -samples.
Differences in findings between our African samples and the West could also be related to the developmental period of emerging adulthood.

In Western countries, emerging adulthood is often described as a life phase of exploration (Arnett, 2007; Roberts & Davis, 2016), whereas young adults in sub-Saharan Africa typically have strong aspirations (and pressures) for education and work to provide for their family and community (Naudé & Breshears, 2025; Rotzinger et al., 2025; Uugwanga et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In Western countries, emerging adulthood is often described as a life phase of exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arnett, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Roberts & Davis, 2016)</ref>, whereas young adults in sub-Saharan Africa typically have strong aspirations (and pressures) for education and work to provide for their family and community <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Naudé & Breshears, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rotzinger et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Uugwanga et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As such, adaptive personality traits and their associations with important life outcomes may differ more in this life phase, with personalityoutcome associations potentially being more similar during other life phases.
Testing this explanation would require a replication of our study in different age groups.
Finally, there is initial evidence that personality traits are functionally different in sub-Saharan Africa compared to Western countries.
For example, personality traits have been found to be less stable in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa than in Western countries (Haehner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, personality traits have been found to be less stable in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa than in Western countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Haehner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, there seem to be cross-cultural differences in how people describe other individuals, with more collectivistic cultures outside the West favoring context-based over dispositional, trait-like descriptions (Church, 2009; Valchev et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Furthermore, there seem to be cross-cultural differences in how people describe other individuals, with more collectivistic cultures outside the West favoring context-based over dispositional, trait-like descriptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Church, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Valchev et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, personality traits are seen as more malleable and situation dependent in non-Western countries (Kanagawa et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Similarly, personality traits are seen as more malleable and situation dependent in non-Western countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kanagawa et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Personality traits may be a less salient topic for young adults in sub-Saharan Africa, used less frequently to describe themselves or others, and thus less relevant to explain individual differences in life outcomes (Thalmayer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Personality traits may be a less salient topic for young adults in sub-Saharan Africa, used less frequently to describe themselves or others, and thus less relevant to explain individual differences in life outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Thalmayer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: If this is true, it may have far-reaching consequences for the cross-cultural applicability of personality theories.

Personality traits might be a less meaningful (though certainly not meaningless) unit of study in sub-Saharan Africa, and contextually-embedded descriptions of persons may be more theoretically and practically useful.

In sum, several factors may account for differences in personality-outcome associations across cultural contexts ranging from methodological factors to functional differences in personality traits across cultural contexts.
To tease apart the different explanations, future research on personality traits in sub-Saharan Africa is needed.

Specifically, studies that examine personality-outcome links in different countries, across different life phases, and with multiple personality trait measures would be needed to better understand cross-cultural similarities and differences in the predictive effects of personality traits.
The present study has several limitations.
First, personality traits and important life outcomes were assessed with self-report measures only.
Self-reports may be prone to biases such as socially desirable responding or acquiescence, biasing the associations between personality traits and outcomes (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007).
text.formatted: Self-reports may be prone to biases such as socially desirable responding or acquiescence, biasing the associations between personality traits and outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Paulhus & Vazire, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, some life outcomes were only assessed with one or few items and analyzed in a dichotomized way, limiting their reliability, and potentially attenuating their effect sizes.
Conversely, personality-outcome associations may have been inflated due to common-method variance.

Future research using multi-method approaches, including peer reports of personality traits and objective and comprehensive assessments of important life outcomes could reduce the impact of these methodological factors.
Second, in the present study, we only examined correlational links between personality traits and important life outcomes.
Identifying robust personality-outcome associations is a necessary first step to better understand the relevance of personality traits across cultural contexts.

Future research testing the causality of these robust associations and identifying pathways mediating these effects is warranted, as the practical relevance of the present findings is contingent on the causality of effects.

Studies examining within-person associations between personality traits and life outcomes could help to reach this goal (Grosz et al., 2024; Jokela et al., 2018; Rohrer, 2018; Stieger et al., 2021; Wright & Jackson, 2023).
text.formatted: Studies examining within-person associations between personality traits and life outcomes could help to reach this goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Grosz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Jokela et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Rohrer, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stieger et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Wright & Jackson, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For such investigations, a high number of assessment waves are needed to provide reliable estimates of within-person effects.
The continuing data collection of ALLS may allow such analyses in the future.
Third, the results of personality-outcome associations may depend on the time interval between assessments (Hopwood et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Third, the results of personality-outcome associations may depend on the time interval between assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hopwood et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We focused on the predictive effects over 2 to 3 years, but longer time intervals between assessments are needed to identify the long-term implications of personality traits.
For example, it could be the case that the consequences of personality traits for relationships or employment require more time to unfold.
Fourth, we considered seven important life outcomes stemming from the health, work, and relationship domains.

However, there are other important outcomes from these and other domains, such as health behaviors, relationship satisfaction, income, job satisfaction, or educational attainment, that we could not examine in the present study (e.g., Soto, 2019).
text.formatted: However, there are other important outcomes from these and other domains, such as health behaviors, relationship satisfaction, income, job satisfaction, or educational attainment, that we could not examine in the present study (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Soto, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, in the present study, we were not able to examine the mechanisms driving personality-outcome associations (i.e., how personality traits express in everyday life and how those momentary personality expressions lead to long-term outcomes).
Future research is thus needed to gain a comprehensive understanding of personality-outcome associations in non-Western countries.
Fifth, for the specification curve analyses, we used the criterion that four of four statistical tests had to be significant to conclude that a personality-outcome link is robust.
However, as there are no established guidelines on how to interpret diverging results in specification curve analysis, this decision rule is somewhat arbitrary.
A more liberal rule (e.g., three of four significant tests) would have resulted in an additional robust link between agency and relationship status.
This again illustrates the relevance of analytic decision for findings and conclusions on personality-outcome associations.
The goals of the present study were to test the cross-cultural replicability of personalityoutcome associations and to probe the robustness of personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa.

Using a large sample of young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, we found that higher levels of agency and communion were linked to better self-reported health and lower levels of anxiety and depression.
While these personality-outcome links were generally robust, specification curve analyses showed that effect sizes depended on country and different ways to capture personality traits.

Interestingly, personality-outcome associations tended to be smaller in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa than in Western countries and some well-established personality-outcome links in Western countries (e.g., with life satisfaction or employment status) were not replicated.

These differences may be explained by methodological factors (e.g., modeling choices) or functional differences of personality traits across cultural contexts, highlighting the necessity of future research on personality traits in sub-Saharan Africa.
Furthermore, differences between personality-outcome associations at the level of lower-order components illustrate the value of more fine-grained personality-outcome examinations.

This figure provides an overview of which analytic decisions influenced the effect size of personality-outcome associations (R² values).
These R² values are the result of linear regression models using effect size estimates as dependent variable and analytic decisions as predictors.
Larger R² values thus indicate that a certain analytic decision explains more variance in the observed differences in personality-outcome associations across model specifications.
Time lag refers to whether personality traits were measured 2 or 3 years before life outcomes.
Manifest/latent refers to whether we used structural equation models or descriptive means to capture personality trait scores.
Country refers to differences across Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa.
Finally, controls captures differences between models using different covariates (e.g., age, gender, education).
